claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNiTi powder blend is nominally equiatomic.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi powder contains FCC Co/Ni/Fe-rich phases and BCC Cr/Ti-rich phases.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces substantial lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
The milling-induced strain and grain refinement lower the energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
Six hours of milling forms a highly strained, nanocrystalline BCC solid solution.
The BCC lattice parameter is expanded by interstitial strain after milling.
The VEC of equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi is approximately 7.5.
At the stated VEC, milling-induced defects destabilize FCC CoCrFeNiTi and promote BCC formation.
Maintaining VEC above the critical threshold for FCC stability and managing atomic-radius mismatch suppress HCP nucleation.
SPS at 1000°C is above the diffusion threshold needed for rapid densification of milled CoCrFeNiTi.
SPS at 1000°C remains below the threshold for excessive grain growth and Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the BCC phase during SPS.
The proposed milling and SPS treatment will produce greater than 99% theoretical density.
The consolidated alloy will have a single-phase or dominant BCC microstructure.
The consolidated alloy will be significantly harder than cast counterparts because of grain-boundary strengthening and retained lattice strain.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi generally has an FCC/BCC or FCC-dominant coarse microstructure with low hardness and high porosity.
CoCrFeNiTi milled for less than 3 hours retains FCC phases and porosity after SPS.
Sintering above 1050°C causes significant grain growth and Ti-rich HCP precipitation.
Milling beyond 10 hours causes enough oxygen or carbon contamination to stabilize brittle oxides or carbides.
Vickers testing at 100 gf can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening and minimize indentation-size effects.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires VEC to remain above a critical threshold for FCC stability while also asserting that approximately the same VEC destabilizes FCC and yields a dominant BCC product.

The boundary predicts increased HCP precipitation above 1050°C, but the falsification rule says that observing increased HCP at 1100°C falsifies the hypothesis, even though that observation would support the stated boundary.
